records.title: P01 — Explicit protected consequence and security objective

scientific_record.Property name: Explicit protected consequence and security objective
scientific_record.Historical origin: Ware-era whole-system security analysis and later requirements/risk traditions; broadened beyond confidentiality labels by systems-security engineering.
scientific_record.Original form: State which information, function or mission must be protected and which confidentiality, integrity or availability condition must hold.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: Controls cannot be judged when the protected object and unacceptable consequence are vague or replaced by generic 'cybersecurity'.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Prevention or bounded acceptance of specified mission, service, safety, privacy, financial, legal or human harms caused through loss of required trustworthiness.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Any relevant intentional actor or compromised component capable of producing the specified consequence; capability and access must be bounded separately.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Control accumulation that does not change a consequential adversarial path; protection of the wrong asset; technically secure behaviour that still permits unacceptable mission harm.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Translate stakeholder consequences into security objectives, invariants, misuse consequences, unacceptable states and decision thresholds; trace controls and evidence back to those claims.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: Always for consequential systems, new exposed capabilities, material trust-boundary changes, or when risk acceptance is requested.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For a low-exposure, reversible change, record the protected consequence and a brief invariant/abuse check rather than producing a full control catalogue.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Named decision owner; system/mission context; asset and dependency inventory sufficient to connect technical state to consequence.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Identity claims are relevant only insofar as they affect the protected consequence; anonymous or environmental threats must not be excluded by default.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Someone must have authority to declare objectives, tolerances and residual-risk acceptance; implementers cannot silently define them by available tooling.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: The objective must bind to the actual architecture, deployment, data flows and dependency versions to which it applies.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Evidence must reveal whether the protected invariant is being approached or violated; otherwise objectives remain aspirational.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Where consequence includes service continuity, recovery criteria and trust-restoration conditions must be stated with the objective.
scientific_record.Expected payoff asserted at this source: Prevents security work from optimising findings, controls or scores that do not reduce the harm decision-makers care about.
scientific_record.Decision or consumer: System owner, product owner, security architect, risk acceptor, operator and assessor.
scientific_record.Known failure modes: Assets are listed without consequence; CIA labels are copied mechanically; objectives conflict; risk acceptance has no owner; non-security dependencies are omitted.
scientific_record.Important criticisms: CIA is useful but incomplete as a universal ontology; objectives can be unknowable, contested or dynamic, and overly broad objectives can justify disproportionate surveillance/control.
scientific_record.How the property evolved: From data-classification and access-control policy to explicit mission/business/service consequences, security invariants and lifecycle trustworthiness claims.
scientific_record.Evolved form in this source: A small, current set of consequence-linked objectives with stated tolerance, decision owner, adversary assumptions, measurable evidence and recovery condition.
scientific_record.Ceremony vs property: A risk register, policy statement or control matrix is optional; the property is an actionable, current consequence-to-claim chain.
scientific_record.Empirical or incident evidence: Incident reports such as S109 and S110 show that failures propagate through identity, architecture, operations and recovery, not merely isolated CVE labels.
scientific_record.Contrary evidence: Objectives can conflict and outcome data are sparse; authoritative guidance establishes disciplined practice, not a universally optimal objective taxonomy.
scientific_record.Open questions: How should objectives be updated when mission dependence, users, adversary capability or external services change faster than formal governance?

records.title: P02 — Bounded adversary and threat model

scientific_record.Property name: Bounded adversary and threat model
scientific_record.Historical origin: Early trusted-system work explicitly assumed malicious users and bounded physical, communications and hardware conditions; later attack-tree, misuse-case and threat-modelling traditions operationalised the idea.
scientific_record.Original form: State hostile capabilities, access, objectives and excluded conditions before arguing that a protection mechanism is sufficient.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: Security evidence is meaningless if the attacker is silently weaker than the real environment or if a named threat is mistaken for a bounded model.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Confidence that required objectives remain protected against specified intentional, adaptive and persistent behaviours, including insider and supply-chain positions where relevant.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Explicit attacker classes, initial access, privileges, knowledge, resources, persistence, collusion, physical proximity and dependency compromise; exclusions are visible assumptions, not impossibilities.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Designs that are secure only because a decisive attacker path was omitted; assurance that tests a toy adversary; inability to explain residual risk.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Represent attacker goals and capabilities, trust assumptions, abuse paths and out-of-scope conditions; use the model to choose architecture, controls and assurance.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: When a consequential decision depends on what an attacker can do, at new trust boundaries, after major change, or when relying on a control with known bypass conditions.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For low-consequence changes, a short trust-boundary and plausible-abuse check can be sufficient; do not instantiate a full template if it cannot alter a decision.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Knowledge of system exposure, dependencies and likely consequence; access to design and operational evidence; an owner for model currency.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Compromised identity providers, operators, workloads and suppliers must be considered where within scope; 'authenticated user' is not synonymous with benign user.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Authority is required to accept exclusions and residual risk; threat intelligence may inform capability but cannot dictate policy.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: The model identifies the exact configuration, deployment and dependency state being analysed and records change invalidators.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Telemetry and incident data should test model assumptions; absence of detection cannot validate absence of attacker capability.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Recovery assumptions must include whether the adversary persists in identities, management planes, update paths or recovery media.

scientific_record.Important criticisms: Completeness is unattainable; analyst subjectivity and knowledge gaps are material; formal overhead can cause abandonment; intelligence is biased toward observed campaigns.

scientific_record.Problem it addressed: Implicit trust in network location, administrative domain, process separation, supplier or management plane permits authority to cross without adequate mediation or containment.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Integrity, confidentiality, availability and accountable control remain bounded when components, tenants, suppliers or users are hostile or compromised.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Adversaries may occupy any untrusted domain and, where modelled, a trusted component; trust is a dependency claim, not a moral judgement.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: An apparently separate component is not an independent boundary; transitive trust expands silently; compromise of a shared control plane defeats many controls.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Map subjects, resources, data flows, authority and enforcement points across process, host, network, tenant, supplier, build and human domains; state what each boundary guarantees.

scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For simple single-user/offline/reversible work, record the few consequential crossings and rely on existing platform isolation where its assumptions are acceptable.

scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Identity assertions are accepted only from stated issuers under bounded proofing/authentication assumptions; identities crossing domains are reinterpreted explicitly.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Each boundary specifies which authority may cross, who can change policy and what delegated authority remains downstream.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Claims bind to deployed topology, runtime configuration, firmware/platform state and supplier provenance; diagrams alone are insufficient.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Boundary crossings and policy decisions need enough logging/measurement to reveal misuse or enforcement failure.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Containment and recovery plans identify which boundaries can be re-established and which trust roots/recovery sources remain clean.

records.title: P04 — Least privilege and authority minimisation

scientific_record.Property name: Least privilege and authority minimisation
scientific_record.Historical origin: Saltzer–Schroeder least privilege, capability/protection-domain work, access-control models and modern short-lived/contextual authorization.
scientific_record.Original form: Give each subject only the privileges needed for the task and only while needed.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: Compromise or misuse of an over-privileged subject converts one foothold or error into broad consequential control.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Reduced unauthorised disclosure, modification, execution, administration and lateral consequence; smaller blast radius after credential or component compromise.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Any principal, process, workload, agent or delegated service may be malicious or compromised while holding legitimate credentials.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Standing or excessive authority permits actions beyond current intent; stale entitlement survives role/task change; shared admin rights defeat attribution.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Minimise scope, resource set, operations, parameters, duration and delegation; separate privilege domains; use just-in-time elevation and explicit exceptions where justified.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: High-consequence actions, multi-tenant/shared systems, automation/agents, remote administration, production access and broadly reusable credentials.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For isolated low-consequence work, platform defaults and a coarse role may be cheaper than elaborate fine-grained policy; still avoid unnecessary administrator/root authority.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Complete task/authority model; usable elevation and recovery paths; policy enforcement that cannot be bypassed by alternate interfaces.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Current subject/workload identity, assurance level and session context must support the granularity claimed.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Entitlement grantors and policy administrators are themselves bounded; delegated authority cannot exceed intended scope.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Entitlements must reflect actual resources, APIs, parameters and deployed policy; reviews compare desired with effective authority.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Use, denial, elevation and abnormal privilege paths need visible evidence; stale/unexercised privilege should be discoverable.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Break-glass and account-recovery mechanisms must preserve availability without silently recreating permanent broad privilege.
scientific_record.Expected payoff asserted at this source: Limits consequence after compromise and makes authorization reasoning, review and revocation tractable.
scientific_record.Decision or consumer: Resource owner, access administrator, service owner, developer/platform engineer, assessor and incident responder.
scientific_record.Known failure modes: Policies become too granular to administer; users share accounts or build shadow systems; stale roles accumulate; nominal rights differ from effective transitive authority; emergency privilege becomes permanent.
scientific_record.Important criticisms: Least privilege is not 'remove every permission'; excessive friction can damage availability, safety and accountability. Empirical outcome evidence for specific entitlement-review programmes is limited.
scientific_record.How the property evolved: From static role restrictions to task-, parameter-, context- and time-bounded authority with automated expiry, workload identity and usable elevation.
scientific_record.Evolved form in this source: Minimise consequential authority across scope, duration, delegation and parameters while preserving a tested path for legitimate work and emergency recovery.

records.title: P05 — Fail-safe defaults and secure failure policy

scientific_record.Property name: Fail-safe defaults and secure failure policy
scientific_record.Historical origin: Saltzer–Schroeder fail-safe defaults, reference-monitor mediation and later fail-closed/availability-aware architecture.
scientific_record.Original form: Base access on permission rather than exclusion and ensure enforcement failure does not silently grant authority.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: Errors, missing policy, unavailable dependencies or exceptional paths can default to access and turn uncertainty into unauthorised action.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Prevents confidentiality/integrity compromise through permissive error paths while explicitly controlling availability and safety consequences.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Attackers can induce malformed, delayed or unavailable inputs and exploit exception/error handling; benign failures also occur.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Unknown or failed authorization becomes allow; cache or fallback expands rights; outage of a policy service blocks a safety-critical function or recovery.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Define per-operation failure semantics: deny, degrade, isolate, queue, require human approval or use bounded cached authority; test dependency failure and recovery.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: Consequential authorization, untrusted input handling, policy/control-plane outages and any path where errors could grant lasting authority.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For reversible low-consequence reads, a degraded or cached mode may be acceptable if scope and expiry are bounded; blanket fail-closed is not required.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Known consequence of denial and grant; dependable local enforcement; tested degraded operation; no hidden bypass path.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Identity/authentication uncertainty must be mapped to the selected failure mode rather than treated uniformly.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Only an authorised policy may choose fail-open/degraded modes; exceptions must be time- and scope-bound.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Failure behaviour must match actual deployment dependencies, caches and policy versions.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Operators need visibility into degraded/fallback state, denied critical work and repeated induced failures.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Recovery must restore intended policy without locking out legitimate administrators or preserving emergency broad access.
scientific_record.Expected payoff asserted at this source: Prevents permissive error exploitation while avoiding simplistic security choices that create unacceptable service or safety failure.
scientific_record.Decision or consumer: Architect, service owner, safety/availability owner, platform engineer, operator and risk acceptor.
scientific_record.Known failure modes: 'Fail closed' becomes a slogan; central policy outage causes denial of service; exception handlers bypass checks; cached decisions outlive context; recovery becomes impossible.
scientific_record.Important criticisms: Security and availability do not always align. A denial can itself be the protected harm, especially in cyber-physical, medical and emergency contexts.
scientific_record.How the property evolved: From categorical deny-by-default to consequence-aware secure failure, bounded degradation and explicit recovery semantics.
scientific_record.Evolved form in this source: For every consequential operation, choose and test a failure mode that minimises combined adversarial and operational harm, with visible degraded state and bounded exceptions.
scientific_record.Ceremony vs property: A configuration checkbox labelled fail-closed is not sufficient; the property is end-to-end failure semantics.
scientific_record.Empirical or incident evidence: S113 illustrates how protective/update mechanisms can create large availability failures; sector guidance S045/S117 requires security–availability/safety co-engineering.
scientific_record.Contrary evidence: No universal fail-safe direction exists; consequence and recovery evidence are domain-specific.
scientific_record.Open questions: How should systems prove that distributed fallback/cached policy does not silently expand authority during prolonged control-plane failure?

scientific_record.Original form: Require two or more independent conditions, roles or authorities before granting a high-consequence privilege.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: A single compromised credential, administrator, build signer or service can perform an irreversible or systemic action.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Reduces unilateral misuse and compromise leverage for critical release, key, financial, administrative, safety or recovery operations.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Adversary can compromise one authority but not all independent conditions; collusion and common-mode compromise are bounded.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Nominal dual approval is performed by one person/account, approvals are not bound to exact action/parameters, or all approvers share the same identity/control plane.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Split approval, execution, key material, policy administration or recovery authority; bind approvals cryptographically/transactionally to exact object, parameters, freshness and context.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: Irreversible/high-blast-radius actions, root/trust-anchor changes, production signing, destructive recovery, high-value transactions and exceptional access.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For a routine, reversible, low-consequence action, a single accountable actor with current authority for the exact effect and suitable logging can be adequate when it satisfies applicable obligations and the stated threat and consequence requirements. Determine any burden preference from the available adequate mechanisms, including an existing dual-condition or multiparty path: compare setup and transition, integration, approval and operating effort, logging and privacy, maintenance, delay and recovery over the decision-relevant horizon. Retain an existing adequate mechanism when change adds burden without a justified benefit. Use independent conditions or authorities where credible independence addresses a specified consequential unilateral-failure path, or where an applicable obligation requires them; multiple conditions need not entail multiple human approval ceremonies. Routine, reversible, low-consequence status alone establishes no comparative cost or usual preference. If comparative burden is not established, leave the ranking unresolved.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Independent identities/channels, low-collusion assumption, usable workflow, exact action binding and emergency path.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Distinct current identities and authentication factors must represent genuinely separate principals, not two prompts to one account.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Approvers must have scoped authority; approval is not execution unless explicitly designed; policy changes require separate governance.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Artifact/action hash, parameters, environment and policy version are bound to approvals.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Evidence shows who approved what, when, under which context, and whether execution matched approval.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Emergency bypass and loss of one authority require tested recovery that does not normalise unilateral control.
scientific_record.Expected payoff asserted at this source: Raises attacker cost and reduces catastrophic single-principal error where independence is credible.
scientific_record.Decision or consumer: System owner, security architect, key/release authority, operations and risk acceptor.
scientific_record.Known failure modes: Rubber-stamp approvals; shared admin accounts; collusion; correlated identity compromise; delay in urgent response; unbound approvals; ceremonial review boards.
scientific_record.Important criticisms: Multi-party control adds latency and can obscure accountability; independence is often assumed rather than tested.
scientific_record.How the property evolved: From multiple conditions for access to parameter-bound, independent, time-limited authorization for specific high-consequence transitions.
scientific_record.Evolved form in this source: The number and independence of required authorities are proportional to consequence; approvals are current and inseparably bound to execution.
scientific_record.Ceremony vs property: A ticket with two names or a standing committee is not the property.
scientific_record.Empirical or incident evidence: S109 and supply-chain mechanisms S062/S065 show the importance and difficulty of independent signing/update roles.
scientific_record.Contrary evidence: Evidence that dual control reduces field incidents is mostly mechanism- and domain-specific; shared infrastructure can defeat presumed independence.
scientific_record.Open questions: What objective tests can establish that two approvals or keys are operationally independent rather than merely administratively distinct?

records.title: P08 — Least common mechanism and common-mode exposure minimisation

scientific_record.Property name: Least common mechanism and common-mode exposure minimisation
scientific_record.Historical origin: Saltzer–Schroeder least common mechanism, protection-domain/security-kernel work and later compartmentalisation, multi-tenant and resilience engineering.
scientific_record.Original form: Minimise mechanisms shared by users or protection domains because shared state and code create information and compromise channels.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: One shared identity, library, control plane, update path, logging service or infrastructure component can bypass nominally layered protections across many domains.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Limits correlated compromise, tenant crossover, covert/unintended channels and systemic blast radius.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Adversary can compromise or manipulate a widely shared mechanism; supposedly independent controls may share the same code, credentials, supplier or management plane.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Defence layers fail together; shared service crosses tenants; central policy/signing/update failure becomes fleet-wide; redundancy is only nominal.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Identify shared mechanisms and trust roots; reduce sharing where consequence warrants; partition administrative domains; diversify only where it breaks credible common mode; test shared dependency failure.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: Multi-tenant systems, fleet-wide management/update, central identity/policy, common libraries, recovery infrastructure and claims of independent defence layers.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For small systems, vetted platform sharing may reduce complexity more than bespoke isolation; document and accept the common dependency.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Architecture/dependency inventory; meaningful isolation; operational capacity to run partitions; evidence about correlated failure.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Shared identity issuers and administrators are explicit trust concentrations; local identities may be needed for recovery.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: No single authority silently controls all supposedly independent layers unless consciously accepted.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Shared code, service, key, image, pipeline and configuration ancestry are traceable.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Telemetry distinguishes local from common-mode failure and survives loss of the shared service.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Recovery sources/control paths must not share the compromise domain they are meant to recover.
scientific_record.Expected payoff asserted at this source: Prevents false confidence from duplicated controls and limits fleet-wide/tenant-wide compromise.
scientific_record.Decision or consumer: Architect, platform owner, supplier manager, resilience planner, assessor and incident commander.
scientific_record.Known failure modes: Excess decomposition creates complexity, inconsistent patching and weaker operations; diversity adds unpatched components; hidden dependencies remain; cost can dominate.
scientific_record.Important criticisms: Sharing is not inherently bad: small, well-analysed common mechanisms can be safer than many complex variants. Diversity without independent maintenance can worsen security.
scientific_record.How the property evolved: From avoiding shared OS mechanisms to analysing common code, vendors, identities, policy planes, cloud regions, pipelines, telemetry and recovery roots.
scientific_record.Evolved form in this source: Minimise or explicitly govern common-mode dependencies in proportion to correlated consequence; prefer small, analysable shared mechanisms and genuine recovery independence.
scientific_record.Ceremony vs property: A count of layers, vendors or zones is not common-mode analysis.
scientific_record.Empirical or incident evidence: S109 and S113 exhibit high-scale common-mode identity/update dependencies; S112 shows a shared upstream component threatening many downstreams.
scientific_record.Contrary evidence: Quantifying correlated cyber failure is difficult; duplicated/diverse stacks can introduce more vulnerabilities and operational errors.
scientific_record.Open questions: How can organisations estimate whether added diversity truly reduces common-mode compromise rather than only multiplying complexity?

scientific_record.Historical origin: Reference-monitor/security-kernel criteria and Saltzer–Schroeder economy of mechanism; continued in minimal TCBs, capability kernels, verified components and memory-safe redesign.
scientific_record.Original form: Keep protection mechanisms and trusted code small and simple enough for analysis, testing and reliable operation.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: Complex privileged code and policy create hidden states, bypasses and assurance scopes too large to understand.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Integrity of enforcement and reduction of exploitable privileged implementation; higher confidence in critical isolation/authorization claims.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Adversary targets any flaw in privileged mechanisms; assurance resources are finite and cannot exhaustively cover a vast TCB.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Security-critical code sprawls across applications, plugins and control planes; 'small' kernel relies on unanalysed firmware/hardware/operations; simplification removes needed checks.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Minimise privileged components, interfaces and policy complexity; use strong isolation; choose safer implementation languages; formally verify narrowly selected high-consequence mechanisms where justified.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: Core enforcement, hypervisor/kernel, cryptographic/update roots, isolation boundaries and high-consequence parsers/protocols.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For ordinary low-consequence business logic, modular testing and memory-safe platforms may be cheaper than radical minimisation or proof.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Clear TCB boundary, stable specification, controlled hardware/toolchain assumptions and operational ownership.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Identity/policy services included in the effective TCB are not excluded merely because external/cloud-managed.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Who may alter TCB code/configuration and deploy it must be tightly bounded.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Exact source, build, firmware, configuration and deployment correspondence are prerequisites for assurance.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Runtime integrity/attestation and failure telemetry should reveal divergence from the assured configuration.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Recovery must restore a known TCB and trust roots; a small TCB does not by itself provide reconstitution.
scientific_record.Expected payoff asserted at this source: Shrinks defect and assurance surface and makes high-value claims tractable.
scientific_record.Decision or consumer: Architect, platform/kernel engineer, verifier, build/release authority and assessor.

scientific_record.Important criticisms: Smallness is not sufficient for security and can conflict with usability/availability. Industrial formal-method success is selected and costly.

records.title: P10 — Open design and secret-minimal architecture

scientific_record.Property name: Open design and secret-minimal architecture
scientific_record.Historical origin: Kerckhoffs's cryptographic principle, Shannon's secrecy-systems treatment and Saltzer–Schroeder open design; extended to public protocols, reviewable mechanisms and minimised embedded secrets.
scientific_record.Original form: Security should not depend on keeping the design or implementation secret; secret keys/credentials remain controlled variables.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: Disclosure, reverse engineering, insider knowledge or widespread deployment defeats mechanisms whose safety rests on hidden design.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Durable confidentiality/authenticity and reviewable enforcement even when algorithms, architecture and code structure are known.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Adversary can learn the mechanism and may obtain documentation/binaries; protected keys and live operational details are not assumed public.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Proprietary obscurity hides defects; public design is mistaken for secure design; publication leaks active secrets or high-risk operational detail; open components receive no meaningful review.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Use publicly scrutinised primitives/protocols where feasible, separate secrets from mechanisms, minimise long-lived secret material, document assumptions and enable responsible analysis.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: Cryptography, widely deployed protocols, critical interfaces and designs likely to be exposed or reverse engineered.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For a local low-consequence mechanism, full public publication is not required; internal independent review and no reliance on obscurity preserve the core.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Sound secret/key lifecycle, competent review community or assessor, and change control.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Identity and authorization still depend on protected credentials/keys; open design does not remove proofing or compromise risk.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Disclosure/publication authority must distinguish reviewable design from operationally sensitive data.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Reviewed description must correspond to deployed implementation/version; public source alone does not prove build or configuration.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Vulnerability reports and telemetry should reveal failures; disclosure channels prevent secrecy from becoming suppression.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Compromised secrets require rotation/revocation and trust re-establishment; design openness does not supply recovery.
scientific_record.Expected payoff asserted at this source: Reduces catastrophic dependence on secrecy of mechanism and permits broader challenge/interoperability.
scientific_record.Decision or consumer: Cryptographic/security architect, protocol designer, assessor, supplier/customer and disclosure coordinator.
scientific_record.Known failure modes: Open source is treated as automatically secure; hidden implementation differs from specification; key management is neglected; disclosure increases exploitation window without remediation.
scientific_record.Important criticisms: Review attention is uneven; public availability creates no guarantee of inspection. Some operational details legitimately require controlled disclosure.
scientific_record.How the property evolved: From algorithm openness to reviewable architecture/protocols, reproducible/provenance-bound implementations and explicit separation of public mechanism from minimal protected authority.
scientific_record.Evolved form in this source: Assume mechanisms will become known; rely on analysable controls and revocable minimal secrets, while managing time-sensitive disclosure responsibly.

records.title: P11 — Psychological acceptability and usable security

scientific_record.Property name: Psychological acceptability and usable security
scientific_record.Historical origin: Saltzer–Schroeder psychological acceptability; modern usable-security research shifted the focus from user obedience to system/work design.
scientific_record.Original form: Protection mechanisms should be easy to use correctly and should fit users' mental models and normal work.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: Controls that impose opaque, repeated or economically irrational burdens induce workarounds, warning habituation, shared credentials and shadow systems.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Security objectives are achieved in the actual socio-technical workflow without transferring unreasonable cost or blame to users/operators.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Adversaries exploit predictable human attention, recovery and workflow constraints; users are bounded-rational actors with legitimate task goals.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Users bypass controls; warnings become rote acknowledgement; recovery channels are weaker than authentication; administrators make errors in overly complex policy.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Remove unnecessary choices, use secure defaults, make consequential decisions legible and rare, prefer phishing-resistant mechanisms, align incentives and test real tasks including recovery.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: Any control that requires repeated human judgement, credential handling, complex administration, warning response or emergency work.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For low-consequence choices, minimise prompts and use reversible defaults; training or documentation alone is not an adequate substitute for design.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: User research, task analysis, support/recovery ownership, accessible interfaces and measurement of real outcomes rather than completion.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Identity mechanisms must be usable across normal and recovery contexts; assurance level must not exceed task need without reason.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Users need clear authority boundaries and an attainable legitimate route; otherwise bypass becomes rational.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Usability evaluation must use the deployed interface/policy and realistic devices/workflows.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Observe abandonment, bypass, support load, warning behaviour and recovery failures without surveillance disproportionate to need.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Recovery is part of the primary design; it must resist impersonation while remaining usable for legitimate loss/failure.
scientific_record.Expected payoff asserted at this source: Reduces predictable bypass and operator error while preserving task completion and adoption.
scientific_record.Decision or consumer: Product designer, identity/security engineer, operator, support owner, workforce/user representative and risk owner.
scientific_record.Known failure modes: Usability becomes aesthetic testing; 'frictionless' flows weaken verification; user studies omit high-stress contexts; training scores substitute for secure outcomes.
scientific_record.Important criticisms: Security burden is context-sensitive; no interface removes all social engineering. Strong controls can still be necessary despite friction.
scientific_record.How the property evolved: From 'make controls convenient' to jointly designing secure defaults, task-compatible authority, legible consequences, phishing resistance and robust recovery.
scientific_record.Evolved form in this source: A control's strength is evaluated end-to-end with real users, incentives, accessibility, failure/recovery and bypass paths; design carries primary responsibility.
scientific_record.Ceremony vs property: A training module, warning banner or 'security culture' campaign is not the property.
scientific_record.Empirical or incident evidence: S099 experimentally observed warning habituation and reduced adherence; S100 found limited efficacy for common embedded phishing-training forms in a large field deployment.

records.title: P12 — Attack-surface minimisation

scientific_record.Historical origin: Trusted-system TCB minimisation, network hardening and software-security design; broadened to APIs, dependencies, identities, build paths and management planes.

scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Reduces reachable adversarial paths and the amount of mechanism that must be patched, monitored and assured.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Adversary can discover and interact with exposed or indirectly reachable interfaces, including through dependencies and compromised insiders.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Unused features remain enabled; hidden management paths bypass policy; decomposition multiplies interfaces; surface counts ignore consequence and reachability.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Inventory exposed subjects/objects/interfaces, disable non-essential capability, constrain input and egress, narrow APIs, remove obsolete components and review surface after change.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: Internet/tenant exposure, privileged services, complex parsers, legacy features, broad egress, agent tools and unmaintained dependencies.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For isolated low-consequence systems, rely on safe platform defaults and remove obvious unused services rather than perform exhaustive attack-surface modelling.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Accurate runtime/dependency/interface inventory; ability to retire features; owner acceptance of compatibility trade-offs.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Exposed authentication/recovery interfaces and machine identities are included, not only network ports.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Administrative and deployment paths count as surface; who can enable features or add integrations is bounded.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Actual enabled configuration and reachable dependency graph, not product documentation, define the surface.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: External and internal exposure monitoring detects newly reachable services, identities and paths.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Removal must preserve needed recovery/diagnostic paths or provide a controlled replacement.

records.title: P13 — Isolation, compartmentalisation and blast-radius limitation

scientific_record.Property name: Isolation, compartmentalisation and blast-radius limitation
scientific_record.Historical origin: Protection domains/capabilities, security kernels, multilevel systems, network segmentation and modern process/container/VM/tenant/service isolation.
scientific_record.Original form: Partition subjects and resources so compromise of one domain cannot directly control or read another.
scientific_record.Problem it addressed: Monolithic authority and shared state permit one vulnerability or credential to become system-wide compromise.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Contains confidentiality/integrity loss, lateral authority and service impact to an explicitly bounded domain.

scientific_record.Problem it addressed: A deputy/service/agent uses its own ambient privilege for a caller's unintended target or parameters.
scientific_record.Security objective or protected conseque: Prevents cross-tenant/object access, unauthorised transactions and escalation through delegated services or automation.
scientific_record.Adversary or threat assumption: Adversary can invoke a legitimate deputy and manipulate object references, destinations, prompts, parameters or token context.
scientific_record.Failure mode it tries to prevent: Valid caller plus valid service yields invalid action; approval is logged but not bound to execution; token audience/scope permits substitution; agent tool call exceeds intent.
scientific_record.Mechanism: Use explicit unforgeable authority/capabilities or narrowly scoped tokens; validate object ownership and parameters at action time; separate data from instructions; bind approvals to exact action.
scientific_record.Trigger or context: Cross-service delegation, payments/destructive operations, cloud roles, callbacks, agents/tools, file/object references and automation with ambient credentials.
scientific_record.Non trigger or cheap path: For an internal low-consequence operation with one resource and no delegation, ordinary local authorization plus input validation may suffice.
scientific_record.Dependencies or preconditions: Canonical resource/action identity, non-ambiguous parameter semantics, local mediation and bounded delegation chain.
scientific_record.Trust or identity preconditions: Caller, deputy and target identities are distinct; authenticated caller does not inherit deputy authority.
scientific_record.Authority preconditions: Delegates can exercise only explicitly conferred rights and cannot re-delegate unless allowed.
scientific_record.Configuration or provenance precondition: Token/approval/action refer to exact current resource, environment, policy and code path; replay/substitution is prevented.
scientific_record.Observability or detection preconditions: Log delegation chain, target, parameters and outcome; detect unexpected cross-domain use.
scientific_record.Recovery preconditions: Revocation/recovery reaches downstream delegated sessions and agent/tool credentials.
scientific_record.Expected payoff asserted at this source: Closes a persistent class of authority bugs that authentication and role checks alone cannot solve.
scientific_record.Decision or consumer: API/identity architect, application developer, transaction owner, agent platform owner and assessor.
scientific_record.Known failure modes: Scope strings are too broad; parameters are canonicalised differently; services trust caller-supplied tenant IDs; ambient cloud credentials remain; approval UI misrepresents action.
scientific_record.Important criticisms: Capability granularity and delegation can be difficult to manage; parameter binding is domain-specific and proofs may omit user-interface deception.
